subject: Copywriting
title: The Attention Economy
description: A quick, practical guide to The Attention Economy.

hook.text: Humans check their phones 96 times per day. Every check is a persuasion opportunity. Attention is the new currency.

buildup.text: Herbert Simon called it in 1971: 'A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.' Social media proved it.

twist.text: Attention-seeking design—infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications—uses the same psychology as slot machines.

climax.text: The attention economy turns every copywriter into a propagandist for engagement.

punchline.text: 96 phone checks daily. Attention is the most competed-for resource.

quiz.question: Who predicted that information wealth would create attention poverty?

details.summary: In the attention economy, human attention is a scarce resource that companies compete to capture and monetize. Platforms design addictive interfaces — infinite scroll, push notifications, autoplay — using the same psychology as slot machines to keep eyes on screens.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the attention economy reveals how digital platforms use persuasion architecture to control behavior. This awareness is the first step toward reclaiming agency over your own attention.
takeaways: Attention is the primary currency of the digital economy
Platform design uses variable reward schedules borrowed from gambling
The average person checks their phone nearly 100 times per day

faq.question: How do platforms capture attention?
faq.answer: They use variable reward schedules — unpredictable likes, comments, and content — that trigger dopamine releases. Infinite scroll removes stopping cues, autoplay eliminates decision points, and notifications create urgency. Every design choice is optimized for engagement.

faq.question: Who coined the term 'attention economy'?
faq.answer: Herbert Simon described the concept in 1971, noting that information wealth creates attention poverty. Tim Wu popularized the term in his 2016 book 'The Attention Merchants,' tracing how industries have competed for human attention since the penny press.
